newsitem.title: USA: U.S. official sees more gene-altered crops.
newsitem.headline: U.S. official sees more gene-altered crops.

text.p: Despite a swirling controversy about the safety of gene-altered crops, a host of new food products are seen coming down the biotech pipeline in the next few years.

Terry Medley, the unflappable Agriculture Department official at the centre of the hot debate over genetically modified crops, says that a handful of so-called transgenic crops now being sold commercially are just the tip of the iceberg in the new biotechnology world.
"Right now we're seeing primarily the first generation of products ... You have to look at this as the first phase of this development," Medley said this week in a wide-ranging interview.

Medley heads the Agriculture Department's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, commonly referred to as APHIS, which is responsible for protecting the health of the nation's plants and animals. APHIS also enforces the agency's relatively new regulatory programme for gene-altered products.

Since the approval in 1994 of the Flavr Savr tomato developed by Calgene Inc., the U.S. biotech food industry has leaped forward with approval requests for more than two dozen genetically modified agricultural products.

Under the complex system of food regulation in the United States, the Agriculture Department, the Food and Drug Administration and the Environmental Protection Agency all have to give clearance on the products.
In the past two years, the Agriculture agency has approved 24 petitions from companies for the marketing of gene-altered tomatoes, potatoes, squash, soybeans, corn and cotton.

Medley predicts that more innovations are on the horizon, ranging from products designed for the cooking consumer -- like a potato that doesn't burn easily -- to crops like cassava and rice, which are used widely in developing nations.

Currently causing a big ruckus are transgenic soybeans and corn that were sold commercially to U.S. farmers for the first time for planting this past growing season, and are now being exported to Europe -- where a storm of controversy has arisen from European buyers.

Medley, who is recognised internationally as a leading expert on biotechnology, said the sharp criticism stems from Europe being at a different stage in their acceptance of gene-altered food products, compared with the United States.

"Here in the United States, we have a system where we are approving these for commercial use ... If you look at Europe, there's very few countries that have developed products that are ready for commercialization," Medley said.

Although rowdy protests against the use of Monsanto's so-called Roundup Ready soybeans have been staged in Europe recently -- including a notable press conference in Rome involving U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman and naked protesters -- Medley thinks that once European consumers see products made from the soybeans, their worries will ease.

Responding to criticism that so far biotechnolgy has focused on crops grown in industrialised countries and has not looked at indigenous crops of developing nations, Medley said the industry is in its early stages and that the technology will eventually be transferred to the third world.
"The knowledge that we gain, even in these early applications in the developed world, can be transferred to situations in the developing countries," Medley said.
For example, Medley said, much work has been done on developing virus-resistant transgenic crops that can in the future be used in developing nations and on the crops of those areas, such as cassava.

Medley said biotechnolgoy is not the only answer to feeding the world's hungry, but that coupled with traditional plant breeding research and other sciences, it will be "a very valuable tool that we must have."
